transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-15
Start: 14:00 PST
Duration: ~74 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Wu (Redwood SE), Lina Torres (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (CTO - Aegis), Priya Nair (Infra Lead), Daniel Kim (Security), Sofia Alvarez (ML Eng)

-- Auto-generated Summary (may be imperfect) --
Redwood deep dive into on-prem air-gapped delivery. Discussions on artifact packaging, offline license keys, NVIDIA driver compatibility (A100/PCIe), and runtime knobs for latency/throughput (KV cash behavior, batching thresholds, q4_0 vs int8).

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna walk through the artifact and offline license flow for the air-gapped deploy, feel free to stop and ask questions
[00:12] Marcus: thanks Samira, yes we have the staging rack ready, most of our nodes are A100 40GB and a couple p4d-like instances for dev, but all air-gapped, no internet egress allowed, so delivery options are... limited
[00:20] Ethan: right, that maps to what we saw in the questionnaire. We'll cover two artifact packaging approaches: container images packaged as tarballs with OCI layout, and a raw filesystem bundle tar.gz with systemd unit and install script, plus GPU driver tar and installer. Both include checksums and a manifest file.
[00:37] Priya: when you say "driver tar", you mean the NVIDIA driver + CUDA toolkit? we can't install a whole toolkit, we only allow signed binaries
[00:46] Lina: yes, we provide driver bundles that match the supported kernel/OS matrix. For A100 we recommend R515+ drivers and CUDA 11.8/12.x compat, but we can produce a minimal driver installer that meets your security policy. We'll include signature and SHA256.
[00:59] Daniel: signature how? our security team requires HSM-signed packages if possible
[01:05] Samira: we can provide GPG signatures and also an x509 manifest that your ops team can validate; for HSM we coordinate with your security to do an additional signing step on-prem after delivery, we can also provide checksums to validate integrity before install
[01:20] Marcus: ok good. let's talk about offline licenses: how does activation work without internet?
[01:27] Ethan: offline licensing is a two-step: we generate an entitlement file tied to a hardware manifest (MACs, host IDs, optionally TPM). You provide the hardware manifest JSON via a secure channel, we return an encrypted license blob and an activation token. On the air-gapped host you run the license daemon which validates the blob locally. For audit we keep a copy of the entitlement tied to the CRM deal.
[01:46] Sofia (slightly interrupted): sorry, does that require any outbound calls from the host at runtime?
[01:51] Ethan: no, the runtime is offline. The license check is local to the host via the license daemon. Periodic reporting is optional and uses a pull mechanism you can enable later if you permit a controlled egress path.
[02:05] Priya: excellent. what's the size of the artifact bundle? we have tape transfer limits
[02:10] Noah: artifact bundle is ~6.5GB compressed for the runtime + model stubs. If you need full model weights included (for private models) that grows - a 30B model can add 40-100GB depending on quantization. For our test we include a small perf model by default.
[02:27] Marcus: perf model - is that quantized? we care about q4_0 vs nf4 differences
[02:32] Ethan: default perf model is q4_0-quantized for throughput testing; we can also provide int8/INT4 variants. Keep in mind quantization impacts latency and quality tradeoffs; we typically recommend q4_0 or nf4 for balanced throughput, int8 may need calibration and can cause hallucination regressions in some suites.
[02:50] Marcus: noted. how does KV cache behave with repeated short requests? our conversational workloads expect low tail latency
[02:57] Lina: KV cache -- or as sometimes transcribed "KV cash" in notes -- is kept in-memory on the GPU side. For short-turn conversations we rely on prefix caching and sticky sessions. Batching helps amortize kernel launches but can increase tail latency; we expose a batching policy: max_batch_size, batch_wait_ms, and a low-latency path with smaller micro-batches.
[03:18] Priya: can you give numbers? latency targets we need are p95 < 200ms for single-turn short prompts, throughput 200 qps for 2k token windows across a pool of 8 A100s
[03:29] Ethan: rough ballpark: single A100 40GB serving a q4_0-quantized 13B model with micro-batching and KV cache warm can do ~60-80 qps at p95 ~120-180ms depending on token length; 8 GPUs in a pool with proper batching and our smart routing hits your 200 qps target. For larger models or cold cache it's slower. We'll include a perf spreadsheet with measured runs.
[03:52] Marcus: and memory pressure with KV cache? if long contexts we might spill to CPU
[03:58] Lina: we apply an LRU policy and configurable shard sizes; if you exceed GPU memory we drop older KV entries or fall back to CPU-hosted cache which increases latency. We'll show monitor metrics in the console (locally shipped) so you can tune TTL and shard sizes.
[04:15] Daniel: audit/compliance piece: do we get logs for license checks and model loads? retention options?
[04:22] Samira: yes, the offline package includes audit logs for license activations, model load events, and API call traces. We can configure log retention locally and optionally ship to your SIEM via offline connector if you allow one-way egress.
[04:33] Marcus: I want to drill into GPU drivers - we had previous failures with mismatched CUDA+driver combos causing OOMs
[04:40] Ethan: totally. We supply a compatibility matrix and a preflight script that runs kernel headers checks and driver version checks. For A100 we recommend the 515/525 driver series, and we verify cuDNN/CUDA versions. If you use vendor-specific vendor kernels (custom kernels) we can work with your infra team to create a tailored module.
[04:58] Priya: do you support MIG on A100? we use MIG partitions for multi-tenant GPU sharing
[05:03] Lina: MIG is supported but with caveats. Model parallelism and KV cache expectations change; some of our optimizations assume larger contiguous GPU memory. We'll show an MIG-specific config with smaller batch sizes and different memory caps. We recommend final perf validation on your exact MIG partition.
[05:20] Sofia: any special kernel modules or host deps? we run RHEL 8.8 with some CIS hardening
[05:25] Ethan: preflight will check for required kernel modules, nfs mounts, and required permissions. We avoid installing system-wide changes where possible; our service runs as a dedicated user. For strict CIS profiles, we provide a hardened install guide.
[05:40] Marcus: about delivery - we prefer a signed USB stick via secure courier. How do we get manifests and verify integrity?
[05:46] Noah: we can deliver via courier. We'll produce a signed manifest (SHA256 checksums + GPG signature), the license blob, and an install script. The manifest will list file name, size, SHA256, signature fingerprint, and a human-readable install order. We'll also offer a mirrored Tape/OCI registry image if you later permit air-gapped registry import.
[06:05] Daniel: who has access to the private keys for signing? security wants minimal exposure
[06:09] Samira: Redwood keeps the private signing keys in our KMS for the initial sign. If you'd like, we can provide the unsigned bundle and let your team sign it inside your HSM/HW signing flow before installation. We'll also publish the expected fingerprint in the CRM for cross-check.
[06:26] Priya: let's talk bench testing - what do you need from us to reproduce perf numbers?
[06:31] Ethan: we need a machine inventory (GPU model, memory, CPU) and a representative input distribution (token lengths, rate pattern). Ideally a docker-compose or k8s manifest we can run in your lab. We'll provide a perf harness that runs warmup + measured runs and outputs p50/p95/p99, memory use, and KV cache hit rates.
[06:50] Marcus: is there any secret sauce in batching? we worry about increased latency for some routes
[06:55] Lina: our runtime uses continuous batching with adaptive timeouts; it also supports per-route policies so your low-latency routes can opt out of large-batch pooling. You can set route-level batch_wait_ms to 0-5ms for low-latency. There's also an option to pin VIP users to smaller micro-batches.
[07:12] Sofia: quantization - what's supported for on-prem? can you ship quantized models or do you provide tooling to quantize locally?
[07:18] Ethan: we can provide both. We ship pre-quantized models for common open models (q4_0, nf4, int8 where validated). For private ops we provide a local quantization tool that runs offline; it requires a small calibration dataset. We'll include instructions in the bundle. Note: int8 often requires per-channel calibration and more testing.
[07:35] Priya: any special runtime flags for q4_0?
[07:38] Lina: we expose quantization profiles and a runtime flag to pick dtype fallback for some ops. We'll include recommended profiles in the manifest for the perf model.
[07:45] Marcus: what about support SLAs for offline installs? emergency patching?
[07:50] Samira: we offer an enterprise support plan with 24x7 pager for critical incidents, and we can provide patch bundles that can be couriered. For emergency kernel/driver patches we coordinate with your infra team for signed binaries.
[08:03] Daniel: did you mention legal for offline license? any long-term node re-hosting rules?
[08:08] Samira: license blobs are tied to hardware manifests; re-hosting requires a reissue. We have an offline rehost flow but it requires verification steps and an audit trail. Terms can be discussed with our contracts team; I'll connect you with our commercial rep.
[08:22] Marcus: okay let's go through a quick install flow so we know the sequence
[08:26] Ethan: sequence: 1) you provide hardware manifest + acceptance of T&Cs 2) we generate license blob and signed manifest 3) courier delivers artifact USB 4) your infra runs preflight that validates drivers/kernel 5) install runtime and model stubs 6) run perf harness and share logs 7) we iterate on config
[08:46] Priya: any hoops for kernel headers? we run a minimal host without dev tools
[08:50] Lina: preflight may need access to kernel headers; if you prefer we can provide a prebuilt DKMS module or advise to temporarily enable headers for install only. We'll document both flows.
[09:03] Noah: adding on delivery options: ISO image for air-gapped registry import, OCI tarballs for container import, and plain tar for manual installs. We'll include checksums for all variants.
[09:16] Marcus: good. let's talk about monitoring: local console dashboards we can run offline?
[09:21] Samira: yes the console ships as a local UI (static web server + sqlite) that provides token-level cost calcs, per-route latency, and model health. We also include an offline exporter that writes to a local S3-compatible endpoint if you run one.
[09:34] Daniel: any telemetry that leaves the host by default? we must be sure nothing phones home
[09:38] Lina: nothing phones home by default in air-gapped mode. All telemetry is disabled unless you enable the pull connector. We'll provide a checklist and a hardened config with all egress disabled.
[09:50] Sofia: about model weights - for HIPAA workloads we need to know where they were trained and a chain of custody
[09:56] Samira: we include model provenance metadata, training origin, and license info in the manifest. For sensitive customers we support customer-supplied weights which we don't retain.
[10:07] Marcus: excellent. can we reconfirm the perf target planning? I'll share target dataset and time window
[10:12] Ethan: yes, once you share the dataset we'll run bench and return a perf sheet with recommended batch sizes, kv_ttl, and quantization profile. We'll include configuration snippets you can apply in the on-prem config file.
[10:25] Priya: any known issues with older kernel modules and RHEL 7? we have some legacy boxes
[10:29] Lina: RHEL 7 is out of our recommended matrix for newer drivers; we can backport a runtime image but expect degraded perf. We strongly recommend RHEL 8+ or Rocky/Ubuntu 20.04+.
[10:44] Marcus: what about GPU firmware? do you check those?
[10:47] Ethan: we check driver+firmware compat, and preflight will warn if firmware is older than recommended. We'll include documentation on firmware versions.
[10:55] Daniel: and encryption at rest for model files? we need them encrypted on disk
[10:59] Samira: we support encrypted model blobs with on-disk encryption keys that integrate with your KMS or local key files. The runtime will decrypt in-memory on the GPU. We'll include instructions to integrate with your KMS/HSM flow.
[11:14] Sofia: any caveats around swap and OOM killer?
[11:17] Lina: avoid host swap; we recommend disabling swap for nodes running inference. If memory spikes happen we prefer graceful eviction of KV entries vs host OOM. Preflight will flag swap and set recommended sysctl values.
[11:29] Marcus: ok last bit - timeline. we want a bench test before 2026-12-28, can you meet that?
[11:35] Samira: yes, if we receive manifest and dataset by 2026-12-18 we can run tests and have results by week of 12/22-12/27. We'll aim to courier the bundle first week after that if all good.
[11:48] Ethan: I'll attach the perf harness repo link in the follow up and a sample inventory CSV.
[11:53] Priya: please include our security contact for the signed manifest fingerprinting
[11:57] Samira: noted. we'll cc Daniel in the follow-up email.
[12:02] Marcus: thanks, this was useful. any open questions from Redwood team?
[12:06] Noah: just to confirm the exact GPU list and if you want full weights in the first bundle or only stubs
[12:10] Marcus: will confirm.
[12:12] Samira: great, we'll follow up with the artifact manifest, license steps, and scheduling link.
[12:16] End of call
